title: Top K Frequent Elements
statement: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the k most frequent elements. You may return the answer in any order.

examples.explanation: 1 appears three times and 2 appears twice, so they are the two most frequent.
With a single element the answer is that element.

hints.content: The problem has two stages. First you need counts, then you need the k largest counts. Which patterns cover those?
Count occurrences in a map, then treat each distinct value as a candidate ranked by its count.
A min-heap of size k ordered by frequency keeps the k most frequent values without sorting all of them.
Bucket sort by frequency is an alternative: group values by count, then walk the buckets from the highest count down until k values are collected.

pseudocode: for each value and its count:
pop the entry with the smallest count
invariant: After processing any prefix of the map, the heap holds the k largest counts seen so far.
whyThisPattern: Counting is the hashing pattern and ranking the top k is the heap pattern. Chaining them is the actual structure of this problem: frequencies build the candidates, and the heap decides which candidates survive.
bruteForce: Count everything, sort the distinct values by count, then take the first k: O(n + m log m). For a large m that sort dominates, while the heap only pays log k per distinct value.
interviewExplanation: I first count the occurrences of every value with a HashMap, then I keep a min-heap of at most k entries ordered by frequency. Whenever the heap exceeds k I remove its smallest count, so after the scan the heap contains the k most frequent values. This gives O(n log k) time.
commonMistakes: Forgetting the counting stage and ranking raw values instead of frequencies.
Ordering the heap by value instead of by count.
Returning heap keys directly when the heap stores counts as keys and values as entries.

solutions.code:
def top_k_frequent(nums, k):
    frequencies = Counter(nums)
    # Ties are broken toward the smaller value so the answer is deterministic. A problem whose
    # answer is not unique cannot be graded: a learner who returns [5] instead of [4] has written
    # something just as correct and would be told they were wrong.
    ordered = sorted(frequencies, key=lambda value: (-frequencies[value], value))
    return ordered[:k]

animationSteps.title: Count first
animationSteps.text: The array 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3 gives counts 1 maps to 3, 2 maps to 2 and 3 maps to 1.

animationSteps.title: Now rank by count
animationSteps.description: The candidates are the distinct values, ranked by frequency.
animationSteps.text: Ranking happens on frequencies, not on values, so the heap stores count and value together.

animationSteps.title: Heap of counts
animationSteps.description: Entries (3,1) and (2,2) are kept, (1,3) is discarded.
animationSteps.text: The heap holds count 3 for value 1 and count 2 for value 2, and the entry with count 1 for value 3 was discarded because it is the smallest.

animationSteps.title: Predict the move
animationSteps.description: A new value arrives with a count of 1 and k is 2.
animationSteps.text: The heap already holds two entries. Choose what happens to a new candidate with count 1.

payload.prompt: Heap is full with counts 3 and 2. A new candidate has count 1. What happens?
payload.explanation: The min-heap removes its own smallest entry, so adding count 1 then popping count 1 leaves the heap unchanged.

animationSteps.title: Heap unchanged
animationSteps.text: After pushing count 1 the heap holds three entries, and popping the smallest removes exactly that entry, so the heap is back to two entries.

animationSteps.title: Answer extracted
animationSteps.description: The heap contains the k most frequent values.
animationSteps.text: The answer is 1 and 2, the two most frequent values of the array.
